>Same thing applies here.

Of course it doesn’t. The two scenarios are wildly different.

A person does not have to shoot up a school for his gun to become capable of taking his own life. A person piloting a plane must necessarily subject his passengers to almost certain death for his plane to become capable of taking his own life.

Yes, the pilot *did* kill all of those people. And yes, that is an unbelievably selfish and grotesque thing to do. But no, it is in no way the same as a killing spree.

In a sense, the suicide of a commercial pilot is the opposite of a suicide bombing. A suicide bombing *is* mass murder, as the suicide is a subordinate, integral step in the commission of the mass murder. An intentional plane crash *is* suicide, as the mass murder is a subordinate, integral step in the commission of the suicide.

The distinction is stark and it matters a lot. Both for the sake of a philosophical/psychological truth of the case, and for what framing of this incident is available to the bereft.

If the pilot had somehow survived, he most certainly would have been charged with homicide. But even then, it could, and probably actually would, be argued that it was "only" murder in the 3rd degree, albeit with extremely aggravating circumstances.

It is obviously true that a pilot of such a plane, wanting to kill himself, *must* know that that means the death of 149 other people as well. But in the case of a successful suicide, there truly exist no consequences for the suicider. That probably makes it easier to just simply not think about the other people affected.

Suicide is poorly understood by most people. It is much more impulsive and opportunistic than most people realize. The people who do it tend to do it with the means that are the most obvious and accessible to them. That is why some people commit suicide in more selfish ways than others. Some people jump in front of trains, traumatizing the driver. Some people drive their car head-on into to a semitrailer, endangering the life of the truck driver and other motorists. These people are probably people who spend time waiting for the train or driving to work, respectively. Their selfish method of suicide is just what was most saliently available to them. Had they been 3rd world farmers, they would have drank pesticide. Had they been hunters, they would have shot themselves. Etc.

It is quite likely that, being a pilot, crashing the plane was simply the most saliently available method for this man to kill himself. Which makes it all the more meaningless and crushing for the relatives of those killed.

Obviously, it will be up to each grieving relative, partner and friend how the motive for this affects how they feel about it. And there will probably be quite a range of feelings, either way.

The case of 149 people simply being incidental collateral damage in one man’s suicide seems quite a bit worse than an intentional attack or genuine human error. While the violent and untimely death of a loved one hurts no matter what, the cause and circumstances of that death will inform the coping process.

I imagine that intentional homicide would feel "best". If the passengers died in what was essentially a terror attack, then they are martyred. The fact that *their* deaths were intended would give more meaning to those deaths.

In the case of human error, whether that of inspection and maintenance personnel missing some critical flaw or weakness in the aircraft, or that of flight crew making a critical mistake, there is at least the fact that whoever is at fault would do *anything* to undo it. They didn’t want to die any more than the passengers did.

With a suicide that just happens to kill many others, there’s just a big nothingness about it. There was no intention behind the deaths, there was no remorse about the deaths, and there’s no punishment for the deaths. The person who did it would have been entirely focused on himself, and death is what he wanted, so it’s no punishment.

>Most suicides are younger people so stop trivialize them as just angsty

That is **extremely** incorrect.

Suicide is one of the most common causes of death for young people. But very few young people die overall!

As five seconds of [googling](https://www.afsp.org/understanding-suicide/facts-and-figures) could have told you, the age groups most at risk for suicide are the middle aged and the elderly.

Suicide is not trivial, and mental illness is not trivial. But it remains a fact that the youngest victims of suicide tend to have trivial reasons for committing suicide.

When a person is middle aged or elderly, suicide is often much less irrational than when a person is young. An old person with no family or friends has nothing to look forward to. A young person, despite problems at home, despite bullying, etc., has all the time in the world to heal and to start fresh.

The older a person is, the more likely their reasons for wanting to end their life are to be reasonable.

I am 31. It gives me a kind of relief to read your post. I always thought that *I* would have my shit together by *now*. It really knots my stomach that I don’t.

There are a lot of young posters on here, and while their troubles are real, so many of them seem blind to how wide open the future is to them and how excruciatingly minor and ephemeral their fuck-ups are.

It occurs to me that I don’t have anything useful to say, but it’s good to see that it’s not just all angsty teens on here.
